newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Crisis deepens for Serbia's Milosevic.
newsitem.headline: Crisis deepens for Serbia's Milosevic.

text.p: Serbia's President Slobodan Milosevic faced a mounting threat to his rule after the biggest protests so far against his annulment of local election results and a fresh broadside from the United States.

A quarter of a million demonstrators, more than 10 percent of Belgrade's population, turned out on a mild wintry Sunday night on the 28th successive day of street protests to try to force Milosevic to accept opposition election victories.
"We are not asking for concessions, but only to get back what is ours," opposition leader Milan Komnenic told the Belgrade rally. "We have patience and we will not back down."
Leaders of the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition said their support was rock solid and they vowed to stage more protests on Monday in a tense face-off with Milosevic over the November elecions.

After the Belgrade rally, about 50,000 students marched through the capital with lanterns and flickering candles "to enlighten a city in political darkness". Belgraders flashed lights in their homes off and on to show their support.

Police kept a low profile during the rally, held in a carnival atmosphere with music, street performers and fireworks, but memories of 1991 when Milosevic crushed the last big street challenge to his rule with tanks were never far away.
Reflecting Washington's increasing concern over the crisis, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for European affairs John Kornblum held talks with Zajedno leaders in Geneva.

"We believe it is now essential for Mr. Milosevic to accept the result of the elections," Kornblum said after meeting Vuk Draskovic, who acccused Milosevic of jeopardising the Dayton peace accord for Bosnia by refusing to acknowledge democracy.
"The Dayton agreement is in danger. Mr. Milosevic must be stopped. Mr. Milosevic must start to think in a democratic way first of all and recognise the election will of the people," Draskovic said.
Milosevic was hailed as a peacemaker at Dayton and a U.N. trade embargo on Serbia was lifted this year to reward him for his contribution towards clinching the accord.
But the United States insisted on retaining an outer wall of sanctions barring Serbia from foreign capital until it improved its human rights record.

Some diplomats said Milosevic apparently hoped opposition protests would run out of steam and the West would overlook his domestic turmoil because of his commitment to peace in Bosnia. "But things are now getting out of hand," one analyst said.

The opposition won a significant victory when a court in the industrial city of Nis ordered the local electoral commission to reinstate an opposition victory. Protest leader Zoran Djindjic said he hoped this trend would continue.
"Zajedno does not agree to re-run elections, we want the results of the elections to be verified," Djindjic told Reuters. "If new elections are called afterwards we have nothing against that."
Opposition protests were also held in at least 30 other towns and cities across Serbia on Sunday and Zajedno leaders hope that many more people will join its future demonstrations.

"The first coach has begun moving, the locomotive wheels are moving. You (Milosevic) can't stop us. If you are smart, move out of the locomotive's way," Djindjic said in a speech. He told the crowd: "See you tomorrow, same time, same place."
